en: Thus have I heard: Majjhima Nikāya 67, the Cātumasutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Cātumā in the Āmalakī grove.
Now at that time, about five hundred bhikkhus headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna had arrived at Cātumā to see the Blessed One.
As those visiting bhikkhus were exchanging greetings with the resident bhikkhus, and were preparing their lodgings and putting away their bowls and robes, they made a loud noise and a great clamor.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Ānanda, what is this loud noise, this great clamor? One would think it were fishermen over a haul of fish!
“Venerable sir, these are about five hundred bhikkhus, headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna, who have arrived at Cātumā to see the Blessed One.”
“Those visiting monks, while exchanging greetings with the resident monks and putting away their lodgings and robes, are making a loud noise, a great clamor.
“In that case, Ānanda, address those monks in my name, saying:
‘The Teacher calls upon you, venerable sirs.’”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. He then approached those bhikkhus and said to them, “The Teacher calls you, friends.
“Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda, and they approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. As those bhikkhus were sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to them:
"Why, bhikkhus, are you making such a loud noise, such a great clamor? You might be thought of as fishermen over their haul of fish!"
“Venerable sir, these five hundred bhikkhus headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna have arrived at Cātumā to see the Blessed One.
These visiting bhikkhus, while exchanging greetings with the resident bhikkhus, and while preparing lodgings and putting away their bowls and robes, are making a loud noise, a great clamor.
“Go, bhikkhus; I dismiss you. You are not to stay in my presence.”

“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. Having risen from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, and kept him on their right as they passed by, they put away their lodgings, took their bowls and robes, and departed.
Now at that time, the Sakyans of Catuma had assembled in the assembly hall for some business or other.
The Sakyans of Catuma saw those bhikkhus coming from afar.
Having seen them, they approached those bhikkhus; having approached, they said this to those bhikkhus:
"Well now, venerable sirs, where are you going?"—"Friends, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has been dismissed by the Blessed One."
“Therefore, venerable sirs, sit down for a moment; perhaps we might be able to persuade the Blessed One.
“Very well, friends,” those monks replied to the Sakyans of Cātumā.

Then the Sakyans of Cātumā approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Sakyans of Cātumā said this to the Blessed One:
“May the Blessed One rejoice in the community of monks;
may the Blessed One welcome the community of monks.
Just as the community of monks was formerly favored by the Blessed One, even so may the Blessed One now favor the community of monks.”
"Venerable sir, there are here bhikkhus who are new, recently gone forth, having only just come to this Dhamma and Discipline.
For them, not obtaining a sight of the Blessed One, there might be a change of state, there might be a transformation.
Just as, venerable sir, for young seeds that do not obtain water, there might be a change of state, there might be a transformation."

In the same way, Bhante, there are here bhikkhus who are new, recently gone forth, having only lately come to this Dhamma and Vinaya; for them, not obtaining a vision of the Blessed One, there might be a change of state, there might be a transformation.
Just as, Bhante, for a young calf that does not see its mother, there might be a change of state, there might be a transformation;

In the same way, venerable sir, there are here monks who are new, recently gone forth, having only lately come to this Dhamma and Discipline; for them, not seeing the Blessed One, there may be a change of heart, there may be a transformation.
May the Blessed One, venerable sir, take delight in the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
may the Blessed One, venerable sir, welcome the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“Just as, venerable sir, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was formerly assisted by the Blessed One, even so may the Blessed One now assist the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Then Brahmā Sahampati,
having understood with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the Blessed One’s mind—
just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm— disappeared from the Brahma-world.
Vanishing from that place, he appeared before the Blessed One.
Then Brahmā Sahampati, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and extending his joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One, venerable sir, take delight in the Saṅgha of bhikkhus."
"Venerable sir, let the Blessed One greet the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Just as the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was formerly favored by the Blessed One, even so may the Blessed One now favor the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

Venerable sir, there are here bhikkhus who are new, recently gone forth, having only lately come to this Dhamma and Discipline; for them, not having obtained a sight of the Blessed One, there might be a change of heart, there might be a transformation."

"Venerable sir, just as young seedlings might undergo alteration or transformation if they do not receive water, even so, venerable sir, there are here monks who are new, recently gone forth, having only lately come to this Dhamma and Discipline; if they do not obtain a sight of the Blessed One, they might undergo alteration or transformation.
Venerable sir, just as a young calf might undergo alteration or transformation if it does not see its mother..."

In the same way, venerable sir, there are here monks who are new, recently gone forth, having only lately come to this Dhamma and Vinaya; for them, not seeing the Blessed One, there might be a change of state, there might be a transformation.
May the Blessed One rejoice in the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
may the Blessed One welcome the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“Just as, venerable sir, the Bhagavā formerly favored the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, even so may the Bhagavā now favor the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
And the Cātumān Sakyan and Brahmā Sahampati were able to inspire confidence in the Bhagavā with the simile of the seed and the simile of the young tree.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the bhikkhus:
“Arise, friends! Take up your bowls and robes.
The Blessed One has been propitiated by the Sakyans of Cātumā and by Brahmā Sahampati with the similes of the seed and the sapling.
“Very well, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and rising from their seats, they took up their bowls and robes.
They approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
As the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Sāriputta, what did you think when I dismissed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus?”
“Thus, Bhante, it occurred to me:
‘The Blessed One has dismissed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Now the Blessed One will dwell at ease, devoted to dwelling in the happiness of the present life; we too shall now dwell at ease, devoted to dwelling in the happiness of the present life.’”
“Wait, Sāriputta, wait, Sāriputta! Remain in this pleasant dwelling in the present life.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
“Moggallāna, what was your thought when I dismissed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus?”
“Thus, Bhante, it occurred to me:
‘The Blessed One has dismissed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Now the Blessed One will dwell at ease, devoted to dwelling in happiness in this very life; and now I and the Venerable Sāriputta shall lead the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.’”
“Excellent, excellent, Moggallāna!
Either I, Moggallāna, should lead the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, or Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, there are these four dangers to be expected for one who descends into water. What four?
The danger of waves, the danger of crocodiles, the danger of whirlpools, and the danger of sharks.”
“Monks, these four fears are to be expected for one who is descending into water.
In the same way, monks, these four fears are to be expected here for certain individuals who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness in this Dhamma and Discipline.
What are the four?”
The fear of waves, the fear of crocodiles, the fear of whirlpools, and the fear of sharks.
And what, monks, is the fear of waves?
Here, monks, a certain clansman goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking: [“I am subject to aging, to illness, and to death”].
“I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs. I am immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering.
Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be known.
When he has thus gone forth, his fellow practitioners in the holy life exhort and instruct him:
‘In this way you should step forward; in this way you should step back; in this way you should look ahead;
in this way you should look aside; in this way you should bend your limbs; in this way you should stretch them out; in this way you should carry your outer robe, bowl, and robes.
It occurs to him:
‘Formerly, when we were householders, we used to advise and instruct others.
Yet these people, whom we consider merely our sons or our grandsons, think that it is they who should advise and instruct us.
Thinking thus, he renounces the training and reverts to the lower life.
“Monks, this is called one who, terrified by the fear of waves, has renounced the training and returned to the lower life.
And what, monks, is the ‘fear of waves’? It is a designation for anger and resentment.
And what, monks, is the fear of crocodiles?”
“Here, monks, a certain son of good family goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking:
‘I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs. I am immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering.
Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.’”
When he has thus gone forth, his fellow-celibates advise and instruct him:
“This should be eaten by you; this should not be eaten by you. This should be consumed by you;
this should not be consumed by you. This should be tasted by you; this should not be tasted by you. This should be drunk by you; this should not be drunk by you.”
What is allowable for you should be eaten; what is not allowable for you should not be eaten. What is allowable for you should be consumed;
what is not allowable for you should not be consumed. What is allowable for you should be tasted; what is not allowable for you should not be tasted.
What is allowable for you should be drunk; what is not allowable for you should not be drunk. You should eat at the proper time; you should not eat at an improper time.
‘You should eat at the proper time, not at the improper time; you should consume liquids at the proper time, not at the improper time;
you should drink at the proper time, not at the improper time.
Then it occurs to him: ‘Formerly, when we were householders, we ate whatever we desired, [drank] whatever we desired…’”
We do not eat what we do not desire; we eat only what we desire. We do not consume what we do not desire;
we consume only what we desire. We do not taste what we do not desire; we taste only what we desire. We do not drink what we do not desire;
we drink only what we desire.
We eat what is allowable, and we eat what is unallowable; we consume what is allowable, and we consume what is unallowable;
we taste what is allowable, and we taste what is unallowable; we drink what is allowable, and we drink what is unallowable; we eat at the proper time, and we eat at the improper time;
we consume at the proper time, and we consume at the improper time; we taste at the proper time, and [we taste] at the improper time.
"Let us drink in the evening; let us drink at the proper time, and let us drink at the improper time.
Even when faithful householders give us choice food and delicacies during the day at the improper time, we seem to be making a mouth-covering of them.
Thus, he renounces the training and reverts to the lower life.
“Monks, this is called one who, terrified by the fear of the crocodile, has renounced the training and returned to the lower life.
‘The fear of the crocodile,’ monks, is a designation for gluttony.
And what, monks, is the fear of the whirlpool?”
In this case, monks, a certain clansman goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking:
"I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs; I am immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering.
Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned."
Having thus gone forth, in the morning he dresses, takes his bowl and robe, and enters a village or town for alms.
With body unguarded, speech unguarded, mindfulness unestablished, and sense faculties unrestrained,
he sees there a householder or a householder’s son provided with, endowed with, and indulging in the five cords of sensual pleasure.
It occurs to him:
"Formerly, when we were householders, we lived indulging ourselves, provided and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure.
Yet, there are indeed riches existing in my family."
‘It is possible both to enjoy wealth and to perform meritorious deeds.
He then renounces the training and reverts to the lower life.
This, monks, is called one who, terrified by the fear of entanglement, has renounced the training and reverted to the lower life.
“‘The danger of the whirlpool,’ monks, is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure.
And what, monks, is the danger of the crocodile?
Here, monks, a certain son of good family, out of faith, goes forth from the home life into homelessness, [thinking]:”
‘I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs. I am immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering.
Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.
Having thus gone forth, he dresses in the morning, takes his bowl and robe, and enters a village or town for alms.
With body unguarded, speech unguarded, mindfulness unestablished, and the sense faculties unrestrained, he sees there a woman poorly dressed or poorly clad.
Having seen that woman poorly dressed or poorly clad, lust invades his mind.
With a mind invaded by lust, he renounces the training and reverts to the lower life.
“Monks, this is called one who, terrified by the fear of the sea-monster *susukā*, has renounced the training and returned to the lower life.
‘The fear of the *susukā*, monks,’ is a designation for women.
These, monks, are the four fears that may be expected here for certain individuals who have gone forth from the household life into homelessness in this Dhamma and Discipline.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The seventh discourse, the Cātuma Sutta, is finished.
